II21A-01.correct_answer: Plants upslope of the spring flowered earlier than plants downslope of it at the same distance from the spring.
II21A-01.explanation: Arceneaux holds that "warm soil is what triggers the early flowering," while Corliss credits "the extra soil moisture the spring supplies." The passage says ground downslope of the spring "is wetter but colder than ground upslope of it at the same distance," so slope position pulls the two accounts apart. The finding that "Plants upslope of the spring flowered earlier than plants downslope of it at the same distance from the spring" puts the earlier flowering on the warmer, drier ground, which Arceneaux's account predicts and Corliss's does not. The finding that "Plants downslope of the spring flowered earlier than plants upslope of it" puts it on the wetter, colder ground, which is what Corliss's moisture account predicts. The finding that "Plants near the spring flowered earlier than plants far from it" restates the pattern that, according to the passage, "Both accounts fit," so it cannot favor Arceneaux. The finding that "Plants far from the spring flowered earlier than plants near it" reverses the observed pattern and supports neither account.

II21A-02.correct_answer: Snails in pools at night left the water more often than snails in riffles at night did.
II21A-02.explanation: Dufresne says the snails are escaping crayfish, "which forage mainly at night," and the passage says pools and riffles "hold similar numbers of crayfish." Her account therefore predicts about as much nighttime climbing in pools as in riffles. Barreto's account predicts more climbing in pools, because oxygen falls "in still water" after dark while "churning riffle water stays well aerated around the clock." The finding that "Snails in pools at night left the water more often than snails in riffles at night did" shows a difference between two habitats with equal crayfish that differ only in oxygen, which weakens Dufresne's hypothesis. The finding that "Snails in pools at night left the water more often than snails in pools at midday did" is predicted by both accounts, since crayfish forage at night and pool oxygen falls after dark, so it cannot weaken either. The finding that "Snails in pools at night left the water more often than snails in backwaters at night did" supports Dufresne: the backwaters "are as still as the pools but hold no crayfish at all," so only the crayfish differ. The finding that "Snails in riffles at night left the water more often than snails in backwaters at night did" also supports Dufresne, since the riffles have crayfish and high oxygen while the backwaters have no crayfish and still water, the opposite of what Barreto's account predicts.

II21A-03.correct_answer: Perch from the south basin's open channel had deeper bodies than perch from its weedy bays.
II21A-03.explanation: Fontaine links deep bodies to protection "from pike," while Castellano links them to feeding "among dense weeds." In the south basin the shallow bays "are choked with weeds but are cut off from pike," whereas the open channel "has no weeds and is patrolled by pike," so bays and channel pull the two accounts apart. The finding that "Perch from the south basin's open channel had deeper bodies than perch from its weedy bays" puts the deeper bodies where there are pike but no weeds, which Fontaine's account predicts and Castellano's does not. The finding that "Perch from the south basin's weedy bays had deeper bodies than perch from its open channel" puts them where there are weeds but no pike, which is what Castellano's account predicts. The finding that "Perch from the north basin as a whole had deeper bodies than perch from the south basin as a whole" restates the difference that, according to the passage, "both accounts fit," so it cannot favor Fontaine. The finding that "Perch from the south basin as a whole had deeper bodies than perch from the north basin as a whole" reverses the observed difference and supports neither account.

II21A-04.correct_answer: Corlan's leaf water content fell from 91% to 85%, while Dalmi's fell from 89% to 81%.
II21A-04.explanation: Avery claims Corlan is more drought tolerant "than every greenhouse variety he tested," and the passage says that the less leaf water content "falls during a drought, the more drought tolerant the variety is." Corlan fell 6 percentage points, from 91% to 85%. The table lists three greenhouse varieties: Bexa (93% to 84%, a fall of 9 points), Dalmi (89% to 81%, 8 points), and Elsin (87% to 74%, 13 points). Dalmi fell the least of the three, so showing that "Corlan's leaf water content fell from 91% to 85%, while Dalmi's fell from 89% to 81%" establishes that Corlan fell less than the most tolerant greenhouse variety and therefore less than all of them. All four choices read the table accurately. The choice ending "while Bexa's fell from 93% to 84%" and the choice ending "while Elsin's fell from 87% to 74%" each cover only one greenhouse variety and leave open whether Corlan outperformed Dalmi, the greenhouse variety that fell least; Bexa's higher final value (84%) does not make it the closest competitor, because tolerance is measured by the fall. The choice ending "while Farrel's fell from 95% to 84%" compares Corlan with Farrel, which the table lists as bred for "Field," so it says nothing about the greenhouse varieties.

II21A-05.correct_answer: Cobb Pond had 14 mosquito larvae per liter, while Elkin Pond had 27.
II21A-05.explanation: Delacorte argues that larval densities differ "mainly" because of backswimmers, "predatory insects that eat mosquito larvae." Support requires a pond with backswimmers holding fewer larvae than a pond without them. The table lists backswimmers as present in Cobb Pond and absent in Elkin Pond, so "Cobb Pond had 14 mosquito larvae per liter, while Elkin Pond had 27" shows the pond with the predators holding about half as many larvae; Cobb Pond is also the slightly warmer of the two (22.7°C versus 22.4°C), so warmer water does not explain the difference. All four choices read the table accurately. The choice "Ash Pond had 6 mosquito larvae per liter, while Cobb Pond had 14" compares two ponds that both have backswimmers "Present," so it cannot show their effect. The choices "Darrow Pond had 16 mosquito larvae per liter, while Brindle Pond had 33" and "Darrow Pond had 16 mosquito larvae per liter, while Elkin Pond had 27" compare ponds where backswimmers are "Absent" in both, so neither difference can be credited to backswimmers.

II21A-06.correct_answer: Corvane seedlings averaged 50 mg in fresh water and 40 mg in salt water, while Abrisk seedlings averaged 60 mg and 45 mg.
II21A-06.explanation: Cardwell argues that in salt water Corvane seedlings "kept a larger fraction of their freshwater mass than seedlings from any other population did." Corvane seedlings kept 40 of 50 mg, or 80%. The other populations kept 45 of 60 mg at Abrisk (75%), 54 of 90 mg at Belloway (60%), 35 of 70 mg at Dunmarra (50%), and 26 of 40 mg at Eskelin (65%). Abrisk kept the largest fraction of the four, so showing that "Corvane seedlings averaged 50 mg in fresh water and 40 mg in salt water, while Abrisk seedlings averaged 60 mg and 45 mg" establishes that Corvane beat the closest competitor and therefore every other population, even though Abrisk seedlings were heavier in salt water. All four choices read the table accurately. The choices ending "Belloway seedlings averaged 90 mg and 54 mg," "Dunmarra seedlings averaged 70 mg and 35 mg," and "Eskelin seedlings averaged 40 mg and 26 mg" each compare Corvane with a population that kept a smaller fraction than Abrisk did, so each leaves open whether Corvane outperformed Abrisk; Belloway's larger salt-water mass (54 mg) is irrelevant because the argument concerns the fraction kept, not mass.

II21B-01.correct_answer: Decks on valley bridges showed more cracking than decks on plateau bridges of the same age.
II21B-01.explanation: Lindahl attributes the cracking to "freeze-thaw cycles," while Grell blames "repeated loading by heavy trucks." The passage says the valley bridges "freeze and thaw far more often each year" than the plateau bridges, "yet they carry far less truck traffic," so valley versus plateau is the contrast that pulls the two accounts apart. The finding that "Decks on valley bridges showed more cracking than decks on plateau bridges of the same age" ties cracking to more freezing and less traffic, which Lindahl's account predicts and Grell's does not. The finding that "Decks on plateau bridges showed more cracking than decks on valley bridges of the same age" ties cracking to heavier traffic, which is what Grell's account predicts. The finding that "Decks on older bridges showed more cracking than decks on newer bridges in the same area" restates the age pattern that the passage says "Both accounts fit," so it cannot favor Lindahl. The finding that "Decks on newer bridges showed more cracking than decks on older bridges in the same area" reverses the observed age pattern and supports neither account.

II21B-02.correct_answer: Blooms were more severe in the northern bays than in the southern bays during the same month.
II21B-02.explanation: Kowal attributes the blooms to "phosphorus washed into the lake from fertilized farmland," while Hartley credits "rising water temperatures." The passage says the northern bays "stay several degrees cooler" than the southern bays "yet they receive the drainage from the region's most heavily fertilized fields," so the two accounts make opposite predictions about north versus south. The finding that "Blooms were more severe in the northern bays than in the southern bays during the same month" links worse blooms to more fertilizer runoff despite cooler water, which Kowal's account predicts and Hartley's does not. The finding that "Blooms were more severe in the southern bays than in the northern bays during the same month" links worse blooms to warmer water, which is what Hartley's account predicts. The finding that "Blooms were more severe in late summer than in early summer within the same bays" restates the seasonal peak that the passage says "Both accounts fit," so it cannot favor Kowal. The finding that "Blooms were more severe in early summer than in late summer within the same bays" reverses the observed seasonal pattern and supports neither account.

II21B-03.correct_answer: On the southern flank, trees on ridges died at a higher rate than trees in the hollows between them.
II21B-03.explanation: Haskins blames carbon dioxide rising "along a fault that crosses the southern flank," while Jallow blames a drought. The passage says the gas "tends to collect in hollows," but that the hollows "also hold more soil moisture than the ridges between them." Haskins's account therefore predicts more deaths in hollows, where the gas gathers, while Jallow's predicts more deaths on the drier ridges. The finding that "On the southern flank, trees on ridges died at a higher rate than trees in the hollows between them" is the opposite of what Haskins's account predicts and fits Jallow's, so it most directly weakens her hypothesis. The finding that "On the southern flank, trees near the fault died at a higher rate than trees farther from it" fits gas rising "along a fault," so it would support Haskins rather than weaken her. The finding that "Trees on the southern flank died at a higher rate than trees on the northern flank at the same elevation" is predicted by both accounts, since the fault crosses the southern flank and the drought "has been most severe on the mountain's sun-facing southern side." The finding that "On the southern flank, older trees died at a higher rate than younger trees growing beside them" concerns tree age, which the passage does not connect to either the gas or the drought, so it does not bear on Haskins's hypothesis.

II21B-04.correct_answer: the prototype stores 180 watt-hours in 1.2 kilograms, while Cell J stores 210 watt-hours in 1.5 kilograms.
II21B-04.explanation: Specific energy is "the energy a cell stores divided by its mass," so the prototype's is 180 / 1.2 = 150 watt-hours per kilogram. Cell H's specific energy, 96 / 0.8 = 120, is also below the prototype's, but the table lists Cell H as sodium-ion, so it says nothing about lithium-ion cells. II21B-06.correct_answer: the average minimum at Kestow was −9.5°C, compared with −13.4°C at Halvern.
II21B-06.explanation: The passage places the top of the cold pool at "about 1,400 meters," so stations above that elevation (Jessmont, Kestow, Lunder) lie above the pool and stations below it (Gessel, Halvern, Ilbury) lie within it. II21C-01.correct_answer: Residents of the Marwick district attended more planning meetings, on average, than residents of the Ronsdale district did.
II21C-01.explanation: Ocampo ties attendance to "how long people have lived in a neighborhood," while Pardo ties it to "homeownership." The passage says that in Marwick households "have lived there for decades but rent their homes," whereas in Ronsdale households "own their homes but moved in within the past five years," so these two districts pull the accounts apart. The finding that "Residents of the Marwick district attended more planning meetings, on average, than residents of the Ronsdale district did" shows long-time renters out-attending recent owners, which Ocampo's account predicts and Pardo's does not. The finding that Ronsdale residents attended more than Marwick residents is what Pardo's homeownership account predicts. The finding that residents of older neighborhoods attended more than residents of newer ones restates the pattern that, according to the passage, "both accounts fit," because older neighborhoods have both longer residence and more homeownership. II21C-02.correct_answer: Turnout declined more in the Mosby precincts than in the Renfield precincts.
II21C-02.explanation: Ortega claims the decline "came mainly from confusion about where to vote after polling places changed, not from distance." In both the Renfield and Mosby precincts polling places moved, so voters in both faced the same kind of change; the groups differ only in that Renfield's new sites are "about as far from voters' homes as the old ones" while Mosby's are "farther away." If "Turnout declined more in the Mosby precincts than in the Renfield precincts," distance made a difference beyond the change itself, which weakens Ortega's claim. The finding that turnout declined more in the Renfield precincts than in the Ordway precincts, where polling places "stayed where they were," shows a change without added distance lowering turnout, which supports Ortega. The finding that turnout declined more in the Quillan precincts, whose sites moved "closer to voters' homes," than in the Mosby precincts compares two groups that both faced a change and cuts against Moraes's distance account, not against Ortega's. The finding that turnout declined more in the Mosby precincts than in the Ordway precincts is predicted by both accounts, since Mosby's sites both changed and moved farther away, so it cannot weaken Ortega's claim.

II21C-03.correct_answer: Residents dropped the final consonant more often at council meetings than at the weekly market.

The finding that "Residents dropped the final consonant more often at council meetings than at the weekly market" ties the dropping to fast but formal speech, which Marchetti's account predicts and Rinaldi's does not. The finding that residents dropped the consonant more often at the weekly market is what Rinaldi's informality account predicts. The finding that residents dropped the consonant more often in casual conversation than in formal interviews restates the pattern that, according to the passage, "both accounts fit," because casual conversation is both faster and more informal. II21D-01.correct_answer: Lowland graves contained more bronze objects than upland graves dug in the same century.
II21D-01.explanation: Ytterberg ties the increase to "wealth brought by a trade route that opened through the basin's lowlands," while Sandahl ties it to bronze growing "cheaper after copper mining began in the surrounding hills." The passage says "the upland villages lay close to the mines but far from the trade route, while the lowland villages lay along the route but far from the mines," so comparing uplands with lowlands at the same time pulls the accounts apart. The finding that "Lowland graves contained more bronze objects than upland graves dug in the same century" matches the villages on the route having more bronze, which Ytterberg's account predicts and Sandahl's does not. II21D-02.correct_answer: Bridges on the Sorle's lower reaches collapsed more often than bridges on the Tyrne's upper reaches.
II21D-02.explanation: Voss claims the collapses came from floodwater scouring the riverbed, so his account predicts more collapses where floods are stronger. The passage says "the Tyrne's floods are violent even in its upper reaches, while the Sorle's are mild even near its mouth," so the Tyrne's upper reaches see stronger floods than the Sorle's lower reaches. The finding that "Bridges on the Sorle's lower reaches collapsed more often than bridges on the Tyrne's upper reaches" shows more collapses where floods are milder, the opposite of what Voss's account predicts; it fits Winslow's account instead, because "tidal salt water reaches the lower reaches but not the upper ones." Each of the other findings compares a lower reach with an upper reach that has both weaker floods and no salt water, because "floods grow stronger downstream" on both rivers and the Tyrne's floods are stronger than the Sorle's. So "Bridges on the Tyrne's lower reaches collapsed more often than bridges on the Tyrne's upper reaches," "Bridges on the Sorle's lower reaches collapsed more often than bridges on the Sorle's upper reaches," and "Bridges on the Tyrne's lower reaches collapsed more often than bridges on the Sorle's upper reaches" are each predicted by both accounts and do nothing to weaken Voss's claim.
